[Release scope and validation](docs/0.39.0-review.md)

Safer fan control, service data that follows the connection, and
restores that are kept until they succeed.

### Changed

- When the window loses the RustWTM service it works locally until the
  service is back, and no longer shows the previous service's
  configuration, kill list, Telegram settings, recorded history or
  incident replay. They are loaded again from the service it reconnects
  to; unsaved Telegram edits are discarded then.
- Switching the service to monitoring ends software fan control at once
  and asks the hardware for its defaults. Apply the fan profile again
  after switching back to enforcing.

### Fixed

- A Telegram save or test message started before the connection to the
  service changed is no longer sent to the service that answers now.
- `wtm` and the window say which side to update when the installed
  service speaks another protocol version: the installed package when
  the service is older, `wtm.exe` from the service's release when it is
  newer.
- Sizes such as `1.5G` are computed exactly instead of in floating point,
  and a size larger than the maximum byte count is refused instead of
  being cut down to it.
- A failed sensor reading no longer leaves the previous readings and
  cooling state shown as current. A fan whose channel disappears or is
  no longer eligible goes back to hardware automatic.
- The hardware helper is started again when it answers a reading without
  a report. When a fan channel reports a different control, the previous
  control is given back to the hardware before the new one is driven.
  On shutdown a failed fan restore is tried once more, and the helper
  exits with an error if a fan is still under software control.
- App power keeps a power plan restore pending while the active plan
  cannot be read, instead of restoring without knowing whether you chose
  another plan; a request that fails to switch keeps the previous one in
  force and named; and a new request is served while a plan you chose
  is kept.
- Core placement keeps a failed restore and retries it on the next pass
  instead of forgetting it, and when an update fails it keeps the record
  of the last placement that worked, so that one is still given back.
- The file locks page and incident replay no longer show a late result
  for an earlier path or an earlier service connection.
- `install.ps1` stops when it cannot remove the previous version's
  directory instead of copying over it, and `uninstall.ps1` removes the
  service's executable and itself last, so a removal that fails half way
  can be run again.

[Release scope and validation](docs/0.38.1-review.md)

Fixes found by running App power against a real power plan, and a safer
PowerShell uninstaller.

### Fixed

- Game mode no longer reports switching to High performance and back
  when that plan is already in use; nothing is switched, saved or
  logged then.
- After you chose another power plan while an App power entry was
  active, a game starting next got no power plan; it now switches as
  usual and gives your plan back afterwards. The *App power* page no
  longer names RustWTM's plan once you chose another.
- The PowerShell uninstaller verifies the service's executable path and
  closes only programs from the selected installation. A native removal
  or cleanup failure stops teardown before files or shortcuts are removed.
  Paths containing brackets are handled literally, and a failed launch
  cleans up the temporary uninstaller.

Ideas taken from Process Lasso: a power plan and keep-awake per app, and
lower I/O and memory priority in rules.

### Added

- **App power** ([design and measurements](docs/app-power.md)): a page
  under *Protect* and `[[while_running]]` entries that, while one of their
  programs runs, switch to a chosen power plan and keep the computer, or
  the computer and the screen, awake. The plan in use before comes back
  when the programs exit, unless you chose another one meanwhile; a crash
  never leaves the machine on another plan. Game mode's plan comes first.
- Rule actions `io_priority` and `memory_priority`: lower a program's disk
  and network I/O priority, or how long Windows keeps its standby memory.

### Changed

- Game mode's High performance plan goes through the same owner as the
  App power entries, so the two never undo each other's plan.
- IPC protocol 20: a 0.37 window and a 0.38 service refuse each other
  until both are updated (the MSI updates both).

[Release scope and validation](docs/0.37.0-review.md)

Core placement: keep an app on chosen cores, keep apps apart while they
run together, or reserve cores for one app while it runs. Telegram reports
only in standard builds and Memory Guard is opt-in in new configurations.
IPC moves to protocol 19: update the service and the window together (the
MSI does both).

### Added

- **Core placement** ([design and measurements](docs/core-placement.md)).
  `[[pin]]` keeps an app on chosen cores: processor numbers (`"0-3,8"`),
  a tier (`"performance"`, `"efficient"`) or a count of the fastest
  physical cores. `[[separate]]` splits the cores between apps that run
  together, by weights, the first app getting the fastest cores, and gives
  them back when one exits. `[[reserve_cores]]` keeps cores for one app
  while it runs and everything else off them. The service writes Windows
  CPU Sets (hard affinity for `strict` entries), by physical core, after
  the rescue core; programs an app starts count as part of it, since
  Windows does not pass CPU Sets on to them. A process that chose its own
  processors is left alone. Every write is recorded, so a restart after a
  crash gives the cores back.
- A **Cores** page under *Protect*: the processors as tiles with who holds
  each, the processes placed and why, and an editor for *Keep on cores*,
  *Keep apart* and *Reserve cores* that previews an entry on the apps
  running now before it is saved. In all 26 languages.
- `wtm cores` shows the service's plan under the processor layout;
  `wtm cores explain <pid>` says why a process has its processors.

### Changed

- IPC protocol 19: the status carries the core plan. A 0.36 service and a
  0.37 window refuse each other until both are updated.
- The rescue core is applied through the core plan: pinned and separated
  apps move off it too while it is engaged.
- Standard builds now limit Telegram to reporting. A service built with
  `telegram-control` requires local opt-in and an allowed private chat for
  system actions. Process arguments are excluded from Telegram's `/info`.
- Telegram checks for configuration changes before handling polled updates.
  Confirmation buttons enforce their five-minute deadline and belong to the
  original chat and message.
- Memory Guard is opt-in in new configurations. Existing explicit settings
  are retained. See the [working-set measurements](docs/memory-guard.md).
- The [installation guide](docs/installation.md) uses a versioned MSI,
  checksum and release workflow attestation. The README links to these release
  notes and the product guides. The MSI includes the installation, usage,
  configuration, Memory Guard and Telegram guides.
- The PowerShell installer checks the registered service path before an
  upgrade and selects running programs by their exact executable paths.
  Portable downloads default to the user profile and ask users to close
  running programs in the target directory.

remaining catalogs, and numbers in the service's messages. IPC stays at
protocol 18, so a 0.36.x service and a 0.36.4 window work together.

  not fit beside them.

  was left; its button now shows only while more than a row is hidden,
  and the faded edge says the rest.

  nothing to say it goes on; the side with columns beyond it fades.

  language ("durchschnittlich 12.5% CPU"); they take the language's sign
  ("12,5%").
- A count of one took the plural noun or verb in Swahili, Hindi, Marathi,
  Gujarati, Punjabi, Telugu, Tamil and Kannada; the singular of the
  well-known tools line says "or" in those and in Bengali, Filipino,
  Indonesian, Vietnamese, Japanese, Korean and Chinese.

The service keeps a week of per-minute history for each disk, network
adapter and GPU, containers keep their last 24 hours and can raise CPU and
memory alerts, About exports a support bundle, the Overview can be
arranged and is redrawn, and the updater holds an update to the publisher
of the build that runs it. IPC moves to protocol 18 (a device's history can
be asked for): update the GUI, CLI and service together; a window and
service of different protocols refuse each other, as before.

### Added

- About has *Export support bundle…*: one text file to send with a
  problem report, with this window's diagnostics, the service's status
  (counts and switches, never names), the last 100 warnings and errors and
  the last 200 warning and error lines of the service log. The whole text
  is shown first, and what is saved is what was shown, through the

A review release: every page was gone over visually and functionally.
Settings no longer rewrites config.toml when it is only opened, a save
made from an older text is refused instead of undoing the other change,
and numbers use the language's decimal sign. IPC stays at protocol 17,
so the GUI and the service of 0.34.0 and 0.35.0 work together.

### Changed

- Every page was reviewed visually in English and Turkish, light and
  dark, wide and compact; what follows came out of it.
- Table cells centre their content in the row, so names, plain labels and
  numbers line up; the Disks folder tree indents across, with every row
  keeping the expander's slot.
- Dialogs have room around their content; About's Check for updates
  button is centred.
- A disabled primary action (Save, Add entry) is an ordinary disabled
  button instead of faded orange, and Panic is red only when it can be
  pressed.
- More below is a rounded pill; in a short window the navigation rail
  keeps the current page in view; a truncated label shows one tooltip,
  not two.
- On a narrow window the Performance timeline shows the time of day, with
  the full date in its tooltip, so its actions stay on one row, German
  included. Overview's Disk card is "Disk & I/O", like the page it opens.
- Kill list and Limits rows use pencil and bin icons for Edit and Remove;
  the AI key field lines up with the fields above it.
- Ports gives spare width to the tool names; App history keeps room for
  its findings; the process inspector's Refresh is an icon; Telegram's
  fields line up; Events messages start under their header and every
  search field says what it searches.
- Turkish: process is "işlem" and service "servis" throughout,
  percentages are written %42 (sliders too), seconds are "sn", and the
  kill list, port categories, AI effort levels and disk read and write
  labels are translated.
- Numbers use the language's decimal sign: Turkish, German, French,
  Spanish, Italian, Dutch, Polish, Portuguese, Russian, Ukrainian,
  Indonesian and Vietnamese write 12,5 and 8,0 GiB. Number fields show
  the comma and accept either sign when typed. Copied diagnostics, logs,
  config.toml and the service keep the point.
- English counts of one read in the singular ("1 startup app",
  "1 TCP port listening").
- On a narrow window, Ports' developer tools table drops the Kind column
  and cuts long tool and program names (shown whole on hover), so Open,
  End and Show stay in view instead of behind a sideways scroll.

### Fixed

- Opening Settings › Service settings could change config.toml without
  any input: number fields pulled hand-set values into their range
  (history_days 730 became 365) and sliders rounded them. Shown values
  are now left alone until the user changes them, and the governor's two
  thresholds can no longer cross and lock the form. Kill list, Limits
  and the rule editor do the same: editing a 2-core limit before the
  first sample no longer saves it as 1 core.
- Clicking a Find handle or DLL hit never loaded the process's details.
- A wait-chain analysis that could not run read "0 threads, 0 blocked";
  it now says it is busy, or that its counts are partial.
- Go to services could open an empty list when Stopped was chosen
  earlier; Details and Properties bring back a hidden inspector.
- A kill-list entry without automatic ending could be added twice, and
  an invalid config.toml showed as an empty kill list.
- Renaming a limit onto another app's limit overwrote it; a refused rule
  save lost the rule being edited.
- Ports' Address column sorted by memory; Overview's Copy Current copied
  nothing for CPU, Memory and GPU.
- Recorded incidents and App history could show another period's data,
  or keep loading for ever; Analyze on a second drive during a scan was
  dropped.
- Network's empty state could not clear a kind filter; About pointed at
  an update bar that Later had hidden; AI's Forget key saved other
  unsaved edits.
- A config save built from an older text (two quick removals in the
  kill list, or an edit made to the file meanwhile) undid the other
  change; it is now refused with a message and the page reloads.
- The tray's Notifications choice is remembered; Restart Windows
  Explorer is offered only on the Explorer showing this desktop, the one
  it restarts.
- Changing tray start while administrator startup was set in a window
  that is not elevated restarted the window and dropped the change.
- The CPU frequency and fan-control confirmations check again before
  applying, in case the service, rights or readings changed meanwhile.
- An update already found stays offered when a later check fails
  offline. Removing an entry from a config.toml that writes the kill
  list, limits or rules as an inline array now says it cannot, instead
  of reporting a removal that did not happen.
- The Network tab reads RustWTM's firewall rules again each minute and
  shows a read error; the Disks tab no longer polls disk activity during
  an analysis or on File owners.
- Inspector filters (Handles, Windows, Memory map) are kept per process
  and say when nothing matches; Containers sort CPU and memory by what
  they show, and "Stopped" is "Not running".
- Sensors' Reset min/max no longer adds the current sample twice; the
  welcome guide's "Continue to overview" goes to the overview; Overview
  offers "Restart as administrator" only to a window that is not
  elevated; "Show hidden devices" counts only devices present.
- Limits could show usage as "-0.00 cores".
- Largest files showed nothing for an unknown modification time, which
  put Show under Modified; it shows a dash.
- A disk's NVMe temperature tile and graph read "42.0 C"; they say
  "42.0 °C", as its Details page does.

More of Process Explorer and System Informer: a system-wide Find handle or
DLL, Find Window's Process, a Windows list, heaps and stacks named in the
memory map, and I/O, network and GPU graphs in the process inspector; and
Hardware specifications becomes a spec sheet. IPC stays at protocol 17,
so the GUI and the service of 0.33.0 and 0.34.0 work together.

### Added

- Processes has Process Explorer's Find handle or DLL, the magnifier at the
  end of its toolbar: every process with a file, registry key or other
  object open, or a DLL loaded, whose name contains the text (three
  characters or more). Processes are searched one
  at a time with this window's own rights and the Handles view's limits,
  and hits arrive as each is done; Stop ends the search, and it stops by
  itself at 1,000 hits or after a minute. The window says how many
  processes could not be opened and in how many names were not all read,
  so that no hits never claims more than was searched. Clicking a hit shows
  the process in the inspector, unless it has exited since. lsass.exe and
  lsaiso.exe are never opened.
- The Memory map names what a process keeps in its private memory: its
  heaps (the default one marked), each thread's stack and TEB, and its PEB,
  with the 32-bit copies of a 32-bit process marked as such, and totals the
  memory of its heaps and stacks. Stacks and TEBs come from the threads'
  own records and the default heap from the PEB; other heaps, which the
  PEB does not list completely on every Windows build, are known by the
  signature in their header. Only those pointers and signatures are read,
  never other memory, and only from processes that allow reading their
  memory; the others still get the full map, with a note that these names
  are missing. Large blocks a heap allocates on their own are not named.
- The process inspector has System Informer's Windows list: the process's
  top-level windows on this desktop with their title and class, visible
  ones first, hidden ones on request, and "Not responding" on a visible
  window that has stopped answering. Switch to restores a minimized window
  and brings it to the front without keeping it on top, and says when
  Windows keeps the focus elsewhere or the window has closed. Each window
  must belong to one of the process's threads, so a newer process with the
  same PID never inherits the list, and nothing is sent to the windows
  while they are listed, so a hung one cannot stall it. Titles often name
  documents, mails or web pages: they are shown, never logged.
- The process inspector graphs its reads and writes (all its I/O, as in
  its Disk read and Disk write rows), network traffic and GPU use over the
  last two minutes beside CPU and memory, as System Informer does. Each
  appears once the process has used it in that time, so an idle process
  keeps a short panel. The graphs share one axis width,
  so their time axes line up, and their scales step in round numbers
  ("20%", "4.0 MiB/s", "1.0 GiB") so each keeps a labelled mark.
- Processes has Process Explorer's Find Window's Process: drag the
  crosshair at the end of the toolbar onto any window and release, and the
  process that owns it is selected and shown in the inspector, with the
  search and filters cleared so its row is in view. The innermost window
  under the pointer counts. Released over RustWTM itself it does nothing;
  over the bare desktop, or over a process not listed yet, it says so.

### Changed

- Hardware specifications is a spec sheet instead of a list of tables: a
  banner with the PC's name and its cores, threads, memory, storage and
  graphics in large type, then an illustrated card per part: the processor
  with a map of its cores and threads, its clock and its caches; memory as
  one drawn stick per slot with its size; drives scaled by capacity with
  their interface and firmware; graphics adapters with their driver; and
  the board with its BIOS. Every field is still under "All details" for
  copying, and parts Windows does not describe are left out rather than
  drawn empty.

  variables by name, as Process Explorer's Environment tab does, with long
  values whole on hover, a copy menu on each value and Copy all; 32-bit
  processes are read from their own block. It is read once on request, by
  this window with its own rights and never through the service, and is
  only shown, never logged or saved, since variables often hold secrets;

  refused.

  the type, value (with the granted access on hover) and name, with files as

  lsaiso.exe are refused. It is read on request, by this window with its

Performance reaches Windows Task Manager parity: every disk, network adapter
and GPU has its own page and graphs, and each page lists what Task Manager
lists under its graph. Processes gains Task Manager's Details columns and a
Threads view, and the system tabs gain Startup impact, publishers, service
groups and Send message. IPC moves to protocol 17 (the sample carries each
adapter's traffic, each GPU's load and memory and more per-process figures);
the GUI and the service must be updated together.

### Added

- Performance lists each physical disk ("Disk 0 (C:)"), each network adapter
  ("Wi-Fi", "Ethernet") and each GPU ("GPU 0") in the rail and the compact
  chip row, each with its own sparkline. The selected device is remembered by
  its model and position rather than by the identifier Windows assigns at
  each start, so it is still selected after a restart; a device that goes
  away falls back to the next one of its kind or to the combined view.
- Disk pages graph active time and the read/write transfer rate, and list the
  active time, average response time, read and write speed and queue length,
  then the model, SSD/HDD and bus, capacity, formatted size, system disk, page
  file and each volume's free space. While the page of an internal SSD is
  open it also shows the drive's temperature with its warning and critical
  limits and, for NVMe drives, the remaining endurance, available spare,
  power-on hours, data read and written, unsafe shutdowns and media errors.
  Hard disks and USB drives show none, since asking could spin them up.
- Network adapter pages graph the adapter's own receive and send traffic and
  list it in bytes and bits per second, the link utilization, adapter name,
  connection type, link speed, MAC address, IPv4 and IPv6 addresses and DNS
  suffix; Wi-Fi
  adds the network name, signal strength and radio standard, read only while
  its page is open because Windows 11 24H2 ties them to location access.
- GPU pages graph the GPU's utilization, four engine graphs (3D, Copy, Video
  Encode, Video Decode first, as Task Manager), and dedicated and shared memory
  against the card's capacity, and list the memory figures, temperature, fan
  speed and memory clock, model, driver version and date and DirectX feature
  level, with the engine search. The rail shows each GPU's temperature with
  its load ("38% (46 °C)"), as Task Manager does.
- The CPU page lists the utilization, current speed, processes, threads,
  handles and up time, the kernel, DPC and interrupt time, interrupts, context
  switches and system calls per second and the processor queue, then the
  model, base speed, sockets, cores, logical processors, virtualization and
  L1/L2/L3 cache sizes.
- The Memory page adds compressed memory and, from the firmware's SMBIOS
  table, the memory speed, slots used, form factor, memory type and each
  module.
- Every device page has a "Copy details" button, as Task Manager's Copy. The
  All resources summary shows the up time.
- Processes offers Task Manager's CPU time and Status (Running, Suspended,
  Not responding) columns, and Disk read and Disk write, the two halves of
  the Disk column (like it, all of a process's I/O); the CPU, I/O and
  Diagnostics column profiles include them.
- Processes also offers Peak working set, Paged pool, Non-paged pool, Page
  faults and Page faults/s (from the same kernel snapshot as the other memory
  columns; the Memory profile includes them), and GPU engine ("GPU 0 - 3D",
  numbered as on the Performance page, shown while the process uses it) and
  Shared GPU memory.
- Realtime priority is offered, after a warning, as in Task Manager. Without
  administrator rights Windows quietly applies High instead; RustWTM reads
  the priority back and reports that.
- Users: "Send message…" in a session's menu shows a message on that user's
  screen, as Task Manager's Send message, without waiting for an answer.
- Processes offers GDI objects and USER objects. They are read only while one
  of those columns is shown, opening each process for a moment with query
  rights; processes this window cannot open show "—", and app rows show the
  sum of what was read.
- Services shows each service's host group (Task Manager's Group column, the
  `svchost -k` group), searchable and sortable.
- App history lists the network bytes each app received and sent in the
  window (Task Manager's Network column; the total, with received and sent on
  hover). The history database gains two columns, added to older databases
  when the service opens them; minutes recorded before have none.
- Settings has "Default start page": the window opens on the chosen page, or
  on the last page used, as before.
- Startup apps shows Task Manager's Startup impact: High, Medium or Low by
  Microsoft's limits (more than 1 s of CPU or 3 MB of disk is High; 300 ms or
  300 KB is Medium), with the CPU and disk figures on hover, or "Not
  measured". The figures are those Windows records for the account at its
  last sign-in (`WDI\LogFiles\StartupInfo`), with the processes a program
  started counted toward it. Only administrators may read them, so the
  service reads them for the connected account (taken from the connection,
  never from the request, so nobody sees another account's) and an elevated
  window reads them itself; otherwise the column shows "—". Command lines in
  those reports are never read out. Startup-folder shortcuts are not matched
  and show "Not measured".
- Set affinity: the process details choose the processors a process may run
  on, out of those of its processor group, as Task Manager's dialog.
- "Go to services" in a process's menu opens Services with the services that
  process hosts; the Services search also finds a service by its process ID,
  and "Open Services" opens the Windows Services console.
- Startup apps lists each program's publisher (the company in its version
  resource), searchable and sortable. It is read once per command and only
  for programs on local fixed drives, never mapped network, removable or
  optical drives; a program on a sleeping hard disk may still wake it once.
- Settings has "Always on top", which keeps the window above other windows
  and comes back after an alert or the tray brings the window forward.
- Performance: right-clicking a disk, adapter, GPU or the battery in the rail
  hides it or moves it up or down; "Show hidden devices" under the rail brings
  hidden ones back. CPU, Memory and the combined views always stay listed. The
  choice is kept across restarts.
- Each GPU engine graph has a menu to choose the engine it shows, as in Task
  Manager; the choice is kept per GPU, and an engine the GPU does not have
  falls back to Task Manager's choice.
- The CPU page lists the current speed of each logical processor, read with
  the same counter as the overall speed.
- "Summary view" under the rail (or double-clicking a resource) shows only
  the resource list, as Task Manager's summary view; choosing a resource or
  "Show details" returns to its page.
- Network adapter pages list the five processes with the most network
  traffic now, and the combined Disk & I/O page the five with the most I/O.
  Windows does not record which adapter or disk a process used, so the
  lists cover all adapters, or all devices (the I/O counters also count
  network and pipe I/O), and say so; per-process network needs the service
  or administrator rights.
- A Battery page, a RustWTM addition, on PCs with a battery: the charge over
  time, power source, charging, time left and battery saver. Capacity and wear
  stay on the Devices page.
- Processes offers more of Task Manager's Details columns: Cycle (the share
  of all processor cycles, idle included), Memory (shared working set), I/O
  reads, I/O writes, I/O other and their bytes (totals since the process
  started, of every kind of I/O), Description, Publisher, UAC
  virtualization (Not allowed, Disabled, Enabled), Data execution prevention
  and Hardware-enforced Stack Protection (Compatible modules only, All
  modules, or either in audit mode), Working set delta (memory) and PF
  Delta (changes since the previous sample), I/O priority (Background, Low,
  Normal, High, Critical) and Package name (for packaged apps), plus an
  Efficiency mode column (On, Off, Windows decides), which Task Manager
  shows only as a status. The security columns and the package
  name are read once per process with the other process facts; I/O
  priority and efficiency mode can change and, like GDI and USER objects,
  are read only while their column is shown. Processes this window may not
  query show "—", and app rows show a value only when every process shares
  it. The CPU, Memory, I/O and Diagnostics profiles include the new columns
  that fit them, and the column menu gains Program and Security groups so
  that no group outgrows a small window.
- "Threads" in a process's details lists its threads, as Process Explorer's
  and System Informer's Threads tab: each thread's CPU since the last read
  (counted like the process CPU column), start address as module+offset,
  state (with the wait reason on hover), current and base priority, and
  context switches. It is read again each second only while it is shown,
  busiest first, at most 50 rows. A thread's start address is read once,
  when it first appears, and needs rights to query the thread; otherwise it
  shows "—". The view is read-only.

### Changed

- The combined Disk & I/O page explains that it graphs the I/O of all
  processes and that each disk has its own page. Combined network and GPU
  views appear only when Windows reports no single adapter.
- IPC protocol 17: `SystemStats` gains `net_adapters` and `gpus`, each disk
  its average response time and queue length, and each process `memory`
  (peak working set, pools, page faults, and the working set and page-fault
  changes since the last sample) and `gpu_detail` (shared GPU memory,
  busiest engine as `{ "luid", "kind" }`), `io` (I/O operations and bytes
  since start) and `cycle_percent`. `wtm list --json` includes them in each
  process. App history rows and summaries gain `net`
  (bytes received and sent), and the new `StartupImpact` request returns the
  connected account's startup usage per program.

### Fixed

- Right-clicking a user session's text now opens its menu; before, only the
  empty parts of the row did.

A visual redesign after the Windows 11 (Fluent) look. No setting, default or
policy changes; IPC remains protocol 16.

### Changed

- Controls and surfaces are rounded (4 and 8 points); the square geometry
  rule is retired. Selected segmented choices are raised chips with a short
  accent underline, and flyouts have soft shadows.
- Every settings page lists one option per row: a Windows icon, the title, an
  optional description and the control at the right edge. On/off options are
  switches showing their state. Service policies use one column with a
  heading per policy; Telegram and AI assistant settings follow the same rows.
- Tables draw no row or column lines by default; both can be switched on under
  Settings → Process workspace. The process table has no outline.
- Charts draw no axes or tick labels: a tinted outline and grid, the top of the
  scale above and the visible time span below. Rate scales move in 1-2-5 steps.
- Performance lists the resources in a rail with their latest reading and a
  one-minute sparkline when the window is wide, and the timeline toolbar is one
  row with icon buttons for sample, zoom and live actions.
- The Processes resource cards form one continuous band; inspector tiles and
  Overview cards are rounded. The Limits and Kill list forms use option rows.

### Added

- AI assistant with your own API key. Right-click a process → *Diagnostics* →
  *Ask AI about it*, or *Ask AI about this PC* in the system overview: RustWTM
  gathers the facts (usage, path, command line, signature, parent and child
  processes, hosted services, ports, startup entries, 24-hour history) and a
  model explains what the process is, whether it looks legitimate, whether it
  is safe to end, and what slows the PC down. Providers: Anthropic (Claude,
  native Messages API), OpenAI, Google Gemini, OpenRouter, Groq, DeepSeek,
  Mistral, xAI, and local models through Ollama, LM Studio or any
  OpenAI-compatible server. Set up in *Settings → AI* (with *List models* and
  *Test connection*) or with `wtm ai setup`, `wtm ai key`, `wtm ai explain`,
  `wtm ai advise`; `--dry-run` prints what would be sent.
- Privacy and safety: off until you agree; API keys are sealed with DPAPI for
  your Windows account; secrets in command lines (passwords, tokens, keys,
  URL credentials) and your account name are masked before sending, command
  lines can be left out entirely, and *Show what was sent* displays the exact
  text. Facts are fenced as data so program-chosen names cannot instruct the
  model, and the model only advises: it is never given control. Keys travel
  only over HTTPS or to this PC, and redirects are never followed with a key.
- The assistant can look things up: when the facts it was given do not settle a
  question, the model may call RustWTM's read-only tools (another process, its
  tree or modules, services, startup programs, connections, history). Bounded
  to six rounds and five minutes, every result masked and fenced like the
  facts, control tools refused, and *Stop* ends it. Models without tool
  support answer from the facts. Turn it off in *Settings → AI assistant* or
  with `wtm ai setup --lookups off`. Ready-made questions (what slows this PC
  down, startup programs to disable, is it safe to end, could it be malware)
  and *Ask AI about it* in the selected process's details.
- MCP server: new read-only tools `process_report`, `process_tree`,
  `process_modules`, `services`, `startup_items` and `app_history`, and the
  prompts `explain_process`, `diagnose_slowdown` and `security_review`.
- Processes: new optional User name, Architecture (x86/x64/ARM64), Elevated and
  File version columns. The Diagnostics column profile includes them. Values
  that this window's rights cannot read show as "—", never as "No".
- Hide system processes: a toolbar switch hides Windows components and services
  (core processes, session-0 programs from the Windows folder,
  System32/SysWOW64/SystemApps helpers). Settings → Processes has editable
  "Always show" and "Also hide" program lists. The selected process always
  stays visible.
- Process tree: nodes can be collapsed and expanded individually. The column
  header menu has Expand all / Collapse all, and there is a "Start the process
  tree collapsed" option.
- Group processes by user: Settings → Processes offers Automatic / Always group
  / Never group for the List view. Automatic groups only while more than one
  person runs programs. A group's context menu offers Manage user accounts and
  "Sign out…", which uses the existing sign-off confirmation.

### Changed

- Verify and reuse complete published website image packages on repeated backfills,
  preserving their bytes when measured frame timings differ in a fresh render.
- Build a versioned website image package from the exact release's fixture-rendered
  interface, and publish it with the installers so homepage highlights and the
  screenshot gallery can follow new stable releases automatically.
- Refresh the product website after successful release publication, release-note
  edits and changelog changes through a repository-scoped GitHub App connection.
- The CPU overload alert closes by itself 15 seconds after the load is back to
  normal, with a visible countdown; *Keep it open* stops it.
- Suspending a process, or every process of an app, now asks for confirmation
  first and explains that its windows stop responding until it is resumed.
  Core Windows processes and RustWTM itself stay protected as before.

### Added

- A skippable five-step quick setup opens on first use and once after each
  version change. Review language, appearance, process layout, tray readouts
  and refresh/update preferences before applying. Existing choices are preserved;
  reopen the setup from Settings at any time. The final review groups choices
  into compact sections with expandable details and direct editing; edited
  sections return to the review without committing the draft.
- Startup apps support case-insensitive name, command, scope and source search,
  combined with enabled/disabled filters, Ctrl+F, Escape and filter reset.
- Choose row and column separators independently across tables. Processes can
  show the Windows file description with the executable name in muted text.
  Name sorting follows the selected presentation and search accepts either name.
- Right-click process headers for sort direction, grouped column visibility,
  fitting widths, column layouts and display options. Data views expose copy,
  navigation and applicable item actions through context menus.
- Process actions group resource limits and diagnostics into compact submenus.
  Disk activity menus copy file paths and readings, and open the selected owner
  in Processes. Process and port menus share viewport-bounded scrolling.

### Fixed

- Overview survives zero-width native startup and measurement passes. Resource
  cards fall back to one column before gutters can produce a negative width.
  Page layout waits for a nonempty client area while visibility and close
  handling remain active. Regression coverage includes every page and recovery
  to a normal window size.
- Restored native window geometry respects the 820×500 minimum, including stale
  64×64 saved windows. Valid sizes, position, maximization and visibility are
  preserved; non-finite dimensions fall back to the normal default size.
- Quick setup keeps language-save errors visible above its scrolling review
  without shifting navigation. Reduced motion also disables automatic scroll
  animations throughout the window and restores normal scrolling when disabled.
- Pages open directly into their content. Settings tabs and cards use the full
  workspace width. Sampling age and the process Inspector menu are in the footer.
- Service thresholds use aligned setting rows with associated accessible labels.
- Installed application and container tables follow the selected row density.
  Container selection highlights the full row and accepts clicks on its values.
- Table separator controls are also available in Appearance settings. Startup
  scope labels use readable account names and the selected-entry toolbar wraps.
